html:
The Eyak are an Alaska Native people of the Copper River Delta on the Gulf of Alaska, around today's town of Cordova. They were always a small nation, squeezed between larger neighbours: the Tlingit to the east, the Alutiiq to the west and the Ahtna up the Copper River.

Their language, Eyak, is the closest relative of the Athabaskan languages; together they form the core of the Na-Dene family. The Eyak fished salmon, hunted seals and traded copper and furs.

Russian traders reached the coast in the late 1700s, and after the Alaska Purchase of 1867 American canneries took over the salmon runs. Disease and marriage into Tlingit and Euro-American families left few speakers. The last native speaker, Marie Smith Jones, died in 2008. The Eyak people continue in Cordova and Yakutat, and work to revive the language.
